summary:
North Macedonia imposes no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Sex between people of the same sex was criminalised until 1996, when decriminalisation was adopted as a condition of Council of Europe membership.

The Law on Prevention of and Protection against Discrimination, adopted in March 2019 with 52 votes in favour and three abstentions, took effect on 22 May 2019 and covered gender identity. The Constitutional Court struck it down on 14 May 2020 on procedural grounds, and Parliament passed a replacement bill on 27 October 2020. The 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code explicitly list sexual orientation and gender identity in the section regulating hate speech, and the constitution and law prohibit discrimination on those grounds in access to government services including health care. The 2019 US State Department human rights report found the government enforced those provisions.

Legal gender recognition is the central unresolved gap for a trans visitor carrying identity documents. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights held that requiring sex reassignment surgery before a gender marker on identification documents could be changed violated the applicant's private life, found a violation of the right of appeal, and awarded 9,000 euros in damages. Non-governmental organisations report that the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. In 2023 the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry, which contained the legal gender recognition chapter, one day before Parliamentary Committee review.

Marriage and partner recognition are closed. Family law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and same-sex couples and households headed by them have no access to the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. In 2014 the government submitted a constitutional motion to define marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption. In January 2015 Parliament approved a constitutional amendment to that effect, together with a requirement that marriage, family and civil unions be regulated only by a two-thirds majority, by 72 votes to 4; the final session did not conclude and the amendment failed. An earlier attempt in September 2013 also failed to reach the required two-thirds majority.

Hate speech remained serious in 2023, with numerous reports and no meaningful state response; the European Commission's country report concurs. In September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years' imprisonment for assaulting an LGBTI activist, applying the Criminal Code's sexual orientation and gender identity aggravating grounds. The 2019 US State Department report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases.

On 29 June 2019, during the first Skopje Pride, about 20 people chased seven activists down the street, pulled them from a taxi and beat activist Bekim Asani, threatening to kill him and the others; police arrested the assailants and opened a criminal investigation. The same 2019 report documents fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student and breaking his nose, which he reported to the principal but not to police. Civil-society monitoring in 2019 recorded violence against LGBTI people, including a verbal assault by a police officer, and noted that most such violence is never reported to police or other institutions, so no reliable rate of violence can be established.

Societal hostility is long-standing and, where measured, severe. A 2002 survey by the Center for Civil and Human Rights found more than 80 percent of respondents viewed homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder that endangered families and about 65 percent considered it a crime warranting a jail term; the same survey found women and rural inhabitants somewhat more liberal. The 2019 US State Department report states that the LGBTQ community is still prejudiced and harassed by society, the media and the authorities, and that the first Pride Parade in June 2019 triggered hate speech on social media. The report also records many reports of public humiliations, worker firings and homosexual teenagers being cast onto the streets after their sexual orientation was revealed.

Official hostility extends to municipal level. In June 2023 the mayor of Strumica, Kostadin Kostadinov, nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organisations and vowed to veto future ones.

Comparative rankings place the country among the weaker performers in Europe. In 2019 it was ranked the tenth worst European country for LGBTQ tourists. In 2024 ILGA-Europe ranked North Macedonia 31st out of 48 European countries for LGBTI rights legislation.

Trans-specific civil society exists and is visible. TransFormA held a March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje to mark the Transgender Day of Visibility under the slogan "we march bravely", and reported a trend of religious institutions being mobilised to scapegoat the country's small trans population. EGAL works on gay and lesbian health issues, and the LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe and ERA's LGBTI Enlargement Review, produced with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia, records that legal gender recognition is the top advocacy priority and that the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the legal gender recognition chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review.

A 2023 study by Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI organisations quantifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination as a measurable drag on the two economies' growth and jobs.

ECRI, a Council of Europe human rights body, called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

In 2012 ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at minus 2 on a 17-to-minus-7 scale, the only Balkan country then in its "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination.

A 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organisers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding.
localsOnly:
The Law on Primary Education, adopted in July 2019, introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The 2019 Criminal Code amendments similarly list both grounds in the hate speech section.

Between 2008 and 2010 lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender individuals were protected from discrimination in employment, but Parliament removed sexual orientation from the protected grounds in early 2010 during a revision of the law. The protection was restored through the March 2019 anti-discrimination law, which was struck down by the Constitutional Court on 14 May 2020 and replaced by a similar bill passed on 27 October 2020.

The LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, provides free legal aid, and EGAL is the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues.
outOfScopeNotes:
No current, trans-specific measurement of societal tolerance was identified. The only attitudinal survey in the inventory dates from 2002, and the available tolerance findings address homosexuality or LGBTI people generally rather than transgender people specifically.

Implementation of the January 2019 European Court of Human Rights judgment is disputed. The Court found a violation and ordered damages, while non-governmental organisations report that gender identity changes are still not recognised in identification documents; no administrative procedure giving effect to the judgment is documented in the inventory.

Enforcement findings rest largely on the 2019 US State Department report, including its assessment that the Skopje public prosecutor was ineffective on hate speech cases; more recent systematic enforcement data are not in the inventory.

No reliable rate of violence against trans or LGBTI people is available. Civil-society monitoring for 2019 records documented incidents and states that most violence goes unreported, so the true incidence is unresolved.
